name: Venda / Tshivenda
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 7 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Meinhof, Carl. 1901. Das Ṭṣ̌i-venda'. Linguistische Studie. Zeitschrift der Deutschen Morgenländischen Gesellschaft 55: 607-682 (separatum Leipzig 1901).
catalog_locator: Sec. 40 b, pp. 654-655 (archive.org Toronto scan of ZDMG 55; same passage in the separatum, p. 48)
catalog_quote: b. Bei der Betonung ist Tonstärke (Quantität) und Tonhöhe (Qualität) zu unterscheiden. Die Tonstärke ist in vierfach verschiedener Hinsicht zu beachten. 1. Der Wortstamm erhält einen Ton, um ihn aus dem Gewirr der Präfixe und Suffixe herauszuheben. Dieser Ton wird von Europäern meist überhört, es ist ein kurzer, scharfer Druck, der auf den Vokal gelegt wird. Der Vokal bleibt dabei kurz. ... Wir nennen ihn Stammton ... 2. Die vorletzte Silbe eines Wortes wird mit einem Ton versehen. Derselbe hat nur euphonischen und keinen etymologischen Grund. Der Ton ist schwer und lang und dehnt regelmässig den Vokal. Ich nenne diesen Ton Dehnung ... Ausserdem werden bei längeren Worten noch mehrfach Silben mit Tönen zur Erleichterung der Aussprache versehen, doch dehnen diese Töne die Vokale nicht in dem Masse wie der Ton auf der vorletzten Silbe. ... Im letzteren Falle trifft wie sehr oft Stammton und Dehnung zusammen. ... 3. Die Sätze haben zur Erleichterung der Aussprache ihren Hauptton und Nebentöne unabhängig vom Wortton. Die vorletzte Silbe eines Satzes, der kein Fragesatz ist, erhält eine besonders starke Dehnung (vgl. die Pausa im Hebräischen). Ich nenne diese Erscheinung „Satzdehnung". ... Bei der Frage verliert die vorletzte Silbe etwas von ihrer Länge, die letzte wird nicht verschluckt, sondern erhält einen starken Nebenton.
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Venda is not in the catalog. this search of works with stress in the title's only item (Mundy & Carroll 2016, Benjamins TILAR 17) is a Glottolog false positive: the reference page says it was linked to Venda by a computerized match on the title string 'adulthood', and the abstract (Coventry Pure portal, saved) is about prosody and dyslexia in adult readers, not the Venda language; irrelevant, priority none. archive.org holds no Doke 1954, Poulos 1990, Ziervogel et al. 1972 or Cassimjee 1992). The best first-hand statement read is already held by the project from the earlier reading and was re-verified against the scanned: Meinhof 1901 ZDMG 55 §40b pp. 654-655 -- short non-lengthening stem accent plus heavy lengthening accent on every word's penult, extra sentence-penult lengthening, final syllable swallowed; corroborated by Meinhof 1915 pp. 75-76, Kusmer 2019 (penult of intonational phrase lengthened; no contrastive length), Downing 2004 (Venda: penult stress, tone, after Doke 1954) and Tzanakakis 2019 (stress not significant, tone is; after Poulos 1990). Still worth acquiring (high): Poulos 1990 A Linguistic Analysis of Venda; Ziervogel, Wentzel & Makuya 1972 Handbook of the Venda Language; Westphal 1962 African Studies 21 'Venda: tonal structure and intonation' (doi 10.1080/00020186208707156); Doke 1954 The Southern Bantu Languages; Cassimjee 1992 Venda tonology. in updated with an addendum.

new_statements.translation: Accent (intensity) must be considered in four respects. 1. The word stem receives an accent to lift it out of the tangle of prefixes and suffixes ... it is a short, sharp pressure laid on the vowel. The vowel remains short. ... We call it stem-accent ... 2. The penultimate syllable of a word is given an accent. It has only a euphonic, not an etymological, basis. The accent is heavy and long and regularly lengthens the vowel. I call this accent 'Dehnung' (lengthening) ... 3. ... The penultimate syllable of a sentence that is not a question receives an especially strong lengthening ... I call this phenomenon 'sentence lengthening'.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Every word carries a heavy, long rhythmic accent on its penultimate syllable, realized as vowel lengthening; in addition the stem syllable bears a short, sharp 'etymological' stem-accent without lengthening. The penult of a declarative sentence is lengthened extra strongly and the final syllable is reduced; in questions the penult is less long and the final syllable gets a strong secondary accent. Modern fieldwork (Kusmer 2019, pp. 220-221) confirms non-contrastive length with obligatory penultimate lengthening at the intonational-phrase/utterance level (variable on utterance-internal phrase penults); Downing 2004 (after Doke 1954) likewise lists Venda as penult stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Meinhof: in longer words additional syllables receive lighter accents that lengthen the vowel less than the penult accent; the stem syllable carries a separate short 'Stammton'. No alternating secondary-stress rule stated.
new_statements.exceptions: Monosyllabic stems with initial nasal compound take the lengthening on the (syllabic) nasal (ndū 'house'); questions: penult loses some length, final syllable gets a strong secondary accent instead of being swallowed; old poetry has a deviant accentuation imitating Kalanga. Kusmer 2019: conjoint verb forms/non-phrase-final words are not lengthened.
new_statements.domain_note: Meinhof states the penult accent for the word (citation forms) and a stronger one for the sentence penult; Kusmer 2019 finds lengthening categorical only on the penult of the maximal intonational phrase (utterance) and variable phrase-internally, i.e. the modern analysis treats it as phrase-level penultimate lengthening in a tone language; Tzanakakis 2019 (after Poulos 1990, Ziervogel et al. 1972) says stress is 'not significant', tone is.
new_statements.identity_note: Meinhof 1901's data come from the Schwellnus brothers (Berlin Mission, Tshakhuma, N. Transvaal), i.e. central/western Tshivenda; Kusmer 2019's fieldwork was in Thohoyandou (standard Tshivenda, Limpopo). Both = vend1245 proper, not a divergent named variety.

new_statements.locator: §40 b, p. 654 (Tonstärke, points 1-2); p. 655 point 3 for phrase-level Satzdehnung
new_statements.reading: First-hand (missionary-informant based) description: two co-existing prominences in Venda -- a short, non-lengthening 'stem accent' on the root syllable, and a fixed, heavy, lengthening 'rhythmical' accent on the penultimate syllable of every word; the penult of a non-interrogative sentence gets extra lengthening (Satzdehnung) and the final syllable is reduced/swallowed. This is the classic Southern-Bantu penultimate-stress/lengthening pattern; Meinhof 1915 (pp. 75-76, also held by the project) restates it in English. Kusmer 2019 (ACAL 47, fieldwork, held by the project) confirms the modern reading: no contrastive vowel length, obligatory lengthening of the penult of the maximal intonational phrase, variable lengthening of non-maximal IP penults, contour tones only on lengthened penults; Downing 2004 table (15) codes Venda as penult stress + tone after Doke 1954; Tzanakakis 2019 (after Poulos 1990, Ziervogel et al. 1972) says 'syllable stress is not significant, but tone is'. For a catalog entry: fixed penultimate prominence realised as lengthening (phrase-level in modern accounts), tone language, no lexical stress contrast.

sources.quote: Die Tonstärke ist in vierfach verschiedener Hinsicht zu beachten. 1. Der Wortstamm erhält einen Ton, um ihn aus dem Gewirr der Präfixe und Suffixe herauszuheben. ... es ist ein kurzer, scharfer Druck, der auf den Vokal gelegt wird. Der Vokal bleibt dabei kurz. ... Wir nennen ihn Stammton ... 2. Die vorletzte Silbe eines Wortes wird mit einem Ton versehen. Derselbe hat nur euphonischen und keinen etymologischen Grund. Der Ton ist schwer und lang und dehnt regelmässig den Vokal. Ich nenne diesen Ton Dehnung ... 3. ... Die vorletzte Silbe eines Satzes, der kein Fragesatz ist, erhält eine besonders starke Dehnung ... sources.note: Sec. 40 b (pp. 654-655) distinguishes four kinds of 'Tonstaerke': (1) 'Stammton' on the stem syllable, a short sharp pressure that does not lengthen the vowel; (2) the penultimate syllable of every word receives a heavy, long accent ('Dehnung') that regularly lengthens the vowel, purely euphonic/rhythmic; in longer words further lighter accents; (3) the penult of a declarative sentence gets especially strong lengthening ('Satzdehnung'), the final syllable is swallowed; in questions the penult loses some length and the final syllable gets a strong secondary accent; (4) special poetic accent.

sources.citation: Cassimjee, Farida & Charles W. Kisseberth. 1984. Downstep in Venda. Studies in the Linguistic Sciences 14(1): 1-29. Urbana: Department of Linguistics, University of Illinois.
sources.quote: Like many other Bantu languages, Venda (spoken in the Zoutpansberg district of the northern Transvaal in South Africa) exhibits the phenomenon known as downdrift ... Venda also exhibits the phenomenon kno\m as downstep ... In her analysis of (simple) nominals, Cassimjee accounts for all of the observed alternations on the basis of underlying representations where there are just High and Low tones and each tone-bearing unit in the nominal is associated with one and only one tone ... In other words, Venda is treated as a true tone language where each tone-bearing unit in a nominal selects either a High or Low tone.
sources.locator: pp. 1-3 (opening summary and sec. 1), SLS 14(1) Spring 1984
sources.note: Venda has two underlying tones (High, Low), each tone-bearing unit linked to exactly one tone; downdrift (H lowered after overt L) and downstep, which the paper argues is always induced by an unrealized Low of three origins: High Tone Spread + Contour Simplification, a floating Low in the tense/aspect system, and Tonal Metathesis; rules Low-Deletion, Meeussen's Rule, High Tone Spread, Contour Simplification; no downstep between penult and final; verbal system data.

All syllables of a prosodic word are monomoraic except for the penultimate, which is regularly lengthened, or bimoraic, on words in isolation or in phrase-final position and which thus is the only syllable that may support a contour tone (apparently always high-low or falling)'.
